column1: # TITLE: Smoking-induced Up-regulation of AKR1B10 Expression in the Airway Epithelium of Healthy Individuals
# SUMMARY: The aldokatoreductases (AKRs) represent a gene superfamily that code for monomeric
column2: soluble NAD(P)H-dependent oxidoreductases that mediate elimination reactions. AKR1B10
column3: an AKR that functions to eliminate retinals
column4: has been observed to be upregulated in squamous metaplasma and non small cell lung cancer
column5: and has been suggested as a diagnostic marker specific to tobacco-related carcinogenesis. In the context of the link of smoking and lung cancer and the enhanced expression of AKR1B10 expression in lung cancer
column6: we hypothesize that enhanced expression of AKR1B10 may be initiated in healthy smokers
column7: prior to the development of any evidence of lung cancer. For this purpose
column8: expression of AKR1B10 was assessed at the mRNA level using microarrays in the large airway epithelium (21 healthy nonsmokers
column9: 31 health smokers) and small airway epithelium (51 healthy nonsmokers
column10: 58 healthy smokers) obtained by fiberoptic bronchoscopy and brushing
column11: as well as assessment in a subset of this population by TaqMan PCR and in endobronchial biopsies by Western analysis and immunohistochemistry. Compared to healthy nonsmokers
column12: ARK1B10 mRNA levels were markedly upregulated in both the large and small airway epithelium of healthy smokers (large airway microarray p<0.0001
column13: small airway p<0.0001; TaqMan large airway
column15: small airway p<0.01). Consistent with the mRNA data
column16: AKR1B10 protein was significantly upregulated in the airway epithelium of healthy smokers as assessed by Western analysis and by immunohistochemistry
column17: with AKR1B10 expressed in both differentiated and basal cells of the normal epithelium. Finally
column18: cigarette smoke extract mediated up-regulation of AKR1B10 in airway epithelial cells in vitro. Thus
column19: smoking per se mediates up-regulation of AKR1B10 expression in the airway epithelium of healthy smokers with no evidence of lung cancer. In the context of these observations
column20: and the link of AKR1B10 to the metabolism of retinals and to lung cancer
column21: the smoking-induced up-regulation of AKR1B10 may be an early process in the multiple events leading to the develop of lung cancer.
